rv.q: Through laughter and unexpected invitations to empathy, it valuably wrestles with the state we're in.
'Mates in Chelsea' feels like a toothless shadow of that high watermark, a bankrupt descendent, destined to be forgotten.

'Mates in Chelsea' stems from a funny concept but in the large space downstairs at the Royal Court, it feels like a satirical comedy sketch that has been overstretched to vapidity in order to fit a full length play.

After enduring this puerile would-be comedy by Rory Mullarkey I'm once again left wondering how an institution that was once renowned for being bold and innovative manages to keep unearthing new writing that is so feeble.

Sam Pritchard’s production feels pacey and energetic, and although it sometimes struggles to pull together all of it’s narrative threads there’s more than enough here to make it an enjoyable evening. ‘Mates In Chelsea’ is braver than it first appears, taking satire to a level where some might not even realise that’s what it’s intended to be.
A lot of the humour depends on the funny foreigner stereotypes — a variety of heavy accents — beloved of British playwrights, and this tends to undercut Mullarkey's serious points.
'Mates in Chelsea' is too disparate in focus to be a straight parody, nor does it have real bite as a comedy of manners.
Mullarkey's script is meandering, unfunny and full of unfinished ideas.

cn.t: Critics find this satirical comedy overstretched and toothless, with a promising concept diluted into a puerile, vapid script that lacks sufficient material for its talented cast to work with.
